subject: chemistry-9
description: Subatomic particles (protons, neutrons, electrons), Thomson, Rutherford, and Bohr models, atomic number, mass number, isotopes, and electronic configuration (Aufbau principle).

questions.question: Atoms of a particular elements have the same:
questions.explanation: Dalton said identical atoms have the same mass and volume.

questions.question: Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed according to:
questions.explanation: Dalton’s theory supported the law of conservation of mass.

questions.question: The indivisibility of atoms was disproved by the discovery of:
questions.explanation: Electrons, protons, and neutrons proved that atoms are divisible.

questions.question: The charge on an alpha particle is:
questions.explanation: Alpha particles carry a +2 charge.

questions.question: The source of alpha particles used by Rutherford was:
questions.explanation: Rutherford used alpha particles from disintegration of polonium.

questions.question: The large deflection of some alpha particles was due to:
questions.explanation: Deflection occurred due to repulsion between positive charges.

questions.question: The continuous emission of energy by electrons would cause:
questions.explanation: Losing energy would make electrons fall into the nucleus.

questions.question: The main drawback of Rutherford’s atomic model arises because:

options.B: o    The nucleus was too large

questions.explanation: Rutherford’s model failed to explain why electrons don’t collapse into the nucleus.

questions.question: Each orbit in Bohr’s model is also known as an:
questions.explanation: Because every orbit has a definite energy, it is called an energy level.

questions.question: Planck’s constant (h) has the value:
questions.explanation: Bohr used Planck’s constant to define quantized energy levels.

questions.question: When an electron jumps to a higher orbit, it:
questions.explanation: Moving to a higher energy level requires absorption of energy.

questions.question: The angular momentum of an electron in nth orbit is:
questions.explanation: Quantization of angular momentum was Bohr’s key postulate.

questions.question: The total energy of an electron in orbit is:
questions.explanation: Negative energy indicates electrons are bound to the nucleus.

questions.question: Instead of orbits, the Quantum Mechanical Model introduces:
questions.explanation: Orbitals represent 3D regions where the probability of finding an electron is highest.

questions.explanation: Energy and orbital radius are directly proportional in Bohr’s model.

questions.question: The more accurately the position of an electron is known, the:

options.A: More accurately its momentum is known
options.B: Less accurately, its momentum is known

questions.explanation: Precise knowledge of one property increases uncertainty in the other.

questions.question: The Uncertainty Principle replaced the concept of:
questions.explanation: The classical orbit model was replaced by probabilistic orbitals.

questions.question: The Uncertainty Principle shows that electrons have:
questions.explanation: Electrons act both as particles and waves, leading to inherent uncertainty.

questions.question: The uncertainty principle demonstrates that electrons:
questions.explanation: Because position and momentum are uncertain, exact trajectories don’t exist.

questions.question: The inability to determine electron paths led to the idea of:
questions.explanation: Orbitals describe the probable zones of electron existence.

questions.question: Atomic models bridge the gap between:

questions.question: Atomic models are essential because they:

options.C: Provide a framework for atomic understanding

questions.explanation: They act as theoretical tools to interpret atomic and molecular behaviour.

questions.question: Despite repulsion between protons, nuclei remain stable because of:
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force overcomes proton–proton repulsion to stabilize the nucleus.

questions.question: The strong nuclear force acts between:
questions.explanation: It acts between all nucleons—proton–proton, neutron–proton, and neutron–neutron.

questions.question: The nuclear force becomes negligible when nucleons are:
questions.explanation: The strong force acts only over short ranges (~10⁻¹⁵ m).

questions.question: The strong nuclear force does not act on:
questions.explanation: Electrons remain outside the nucleus and are not affected by nuclear forces.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle has the smallest mass?
questions.explanation: The electron is approximately 1/1836 the mass of a proton. 1.6726×10⁻²⁷ 1.6749×10⁻³¹ 32. The mass of a proton is 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg 2.0×10⁻²⁷ kg ○ ○ ○ ○ kg kg approximately: Answer: (B) 1.6726×10⁻²⁷ kg

questions.question: The mass of a proton is approximately:
questions.explanation: Proton mass is ~1 atomic mass unit (amu), roughly 1.6726×10⁻²⁷ kg.

questions.question: Which force prevents the nucleus from breaking apart?
questions.explanation: Strong nuclear force overcomes proton–proton repulsion and stabilizes the nucleus.

questions.question: The charge-to-mass ratio of an electron is:
questions.explanation: Electrons’ charge is negative and its mass is extremely small compared to nucleons.

questions.question: The mass of an electron in atomic mass units (amu) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Electron mass is tiny compared to protons and neutrons (~1/1836 amu).

questions.question: The attraction between electrons and protons keeps atoms:
questions.explanation: Equal proton and electron numbers ensure atomic stability and neutrality.

questions.question: If the electrostatic attraction between protons and electrons vanished, atoms would:
questions.explanation: Without electrostatic force, electrons would escape, breaking the atom apart.

questions.question: In an electric field, protons are deflected toward the:
questions.explanation: Protons carry a positive charge, so they are attracted to the negative plate.

questions.question: When protons and electrons travel at the same L speed, electrons are deflected:
questions.explanation: Because of their lighter mass, electrons deviate more than heavy protons.

questions.question: If electrons and protons Cu move in opposite directions sa in an electric field, their paths will:
questions.explanation: Positive and negative particles bend in opposite directions due to opposite charges.

questions.question: Deflection of a charged particle in an electric field depends on:
questions.explanation: The greater the charge and the smaller the mass, the greater the deflection.

questions.question: When the number of electrons equals the number of protons, the atom’s net charge is:
questions.explanation: Equal but opposite charges cancel, resulting in zero net charge.

questions.question: In a neutral atom, removing a proton would make it:
questions.explanation: Removing a positive charge leaves an excess of electrons, creating a negative atom.

questions.question: Charge neutrality is maintained in an atom by:
questions.explanation: The balance between proton and electron charges keeps the atom neutral.

questions.question: Radioactive decay occurs when an atom has:
questions.explanation: Unstable combinations of neutrons and protons cause decay.

questions.question: Hydrogen-3 (tritium) is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Tritium is a radioactive form of hydrogen with two neutrons.

questions.question: The number of protons in isotopes of an element is:
questions.explanation: Protons define the element, so their number remains constant.

questions.question: Carbon-14 is widely used in:
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 helps estimate the age of ancient organic materials. Chemically Electrically Electron Nuclear 49. Uranium-238 is a ○ ○ ○ ○ unstable unstable deficient unstable radioisotope that is: Answer: (D) Nuclear unstable

questions.question: Uranium-238 is a radioisotope that is:
questions.explanation: Uranium-238 has an unstable nucleus that undergoes radioactive decay.

questions.question: In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of:
questions.explanation: An equal numbers of protons and electrons balance the atom’s charge.

questions.question: The atom of hydrogen has how many protons?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen’s nucleus contains a single proton, so Z = 1.

questions.question: The atomic number of carbon is 6, meaning it has:
questions.explanation: Carbon’s atomic number equals its six positively charged protons.

questions.question: The number of electrons in a neutral oxygen atom is:
questions.explanation: Oxygen has 8 protons, so it also has 8 electrons.

questions.question: The atomic number of an ion changes only when:
questions.explanation: Only altering proton count changes the element’s atomic number.

questions.question: The number of protons defines the element’s:
questions.explanation: The proton count determines the element’s exact position.

questions.question: Which of the following elements has 20 protons?
questions.explanation: Calcium’s atomic number is 20.

questions.question: In neutral atoms, the proton number also indicates:
questions.explanation: Neutral atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons.

questions.question: Elements with the same number of protons but different neutrons are called:
questions.explanation: Isotopes differ only in neutron count, not proton count.

questions.question: What do we call the phenomenon in which an unstable nucleus emits particles to become more stable?
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is the process by which unstable nuclei emit particles until they reach stability

questions.question: Which statement best describes radioactive decay?
questions.explanation: Decay continues until stability is reached

questions.question: Why does C-14 exist in living organisms?
questions.explanation: Organisms take in CO₂ containing C-14

questions.question: Uranium-238 eventually becomes ______ after its decay series
questions.explanation: U-238 decays through steps to stable Pb-206

questions.question: Carbon-14 transforms into which element after decay?
questions.explanation: C-14 decays to N-14 via beta decay

questions.question: Relative atomic mass compares the mass of an atom to the mass of which isotope?
questions.explanation: The C-12 isotope is the agreed international reference for comparing all atomic masses 65. Which instrument Optical Electron Mass accurately determined Atomic clock ○ ○ ○ ○ spectrometer microscope spectrometer the mass of the C-12 isotope? Answer: (D) Mass spectrometer

questions.question: Which instrument accurately determined the mass of the C-12 isotope?
questions.explanation: Mass spectrometers precisely measure atomic and molecular masses using charged particle separation

questions.question: The mass of other elements is compared to C-12 to determine their _____.
questions.explanation: Relative atomic mass is a comparison of an atom’s mass with the mass of C-12

questions.question: Carbon-12 is described as a “light isotope” because it

options.B: Has the lowest mass among carbons

questions.explanation: C-12 is the lightest stable isotope of carbon used as a mass reference

questions.question: The C-12 isotope contains how many neutrons
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, giving it mass number 12

questions.question: Relative atomic mass uses C-12 as the baseline because its mass is
questions.explanation: The mass of C-12 is fixed at exactly 12 amu, serving as a perfect reference

questions.question: Why is the mass of electrons ignored in atomic mass calculations

options.C: Electron mass E is extremely small

questions.explanation: Electron mass is negligible compared to protons and neutrons.

questions.question: Isotopes differ from one another in their _____.
questions.explanation: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, causing different mass numbers.

questions.question: Isotopes have different mass numbers because they have different _____.
questions.explanation: Variation in neutron count changes the mass number.

questions.question: Why are isotopes considered atoms of the same element?

options.C: They have       T same neutrons       el

questions.explanation: Identity of an element comes from its number of protons, which isotopes share.

questions.question: Which hydrogen isotope contains no neutrons?
questions.explanation: Protium (H-1) consists of only one proton and no neutron.

questions.question: Why is tritium rare in nature?

options.C: It reacts     It instantly with air

questions.explanation: Tritium is radioactive and decays rapidly due to instability.

questions.question: Water containing deuterium instead of protium is called _____.
questions.explanation: When H-2 replaces H-1 in water, it becomes heavy water (D₂O).

questions.question: What is the melting point of heavy water?
questions.explanation: Heavy water has a slightly higher melting point than normal water.

questions.question: The boiling point of heavy water is _____.
questions.explanation: Heavy water boils at 101.2°C due to increased mass.

questions.question: Which hydrogen isotope is radioactive?
questions.explanation: Tritium is the only radioactive isotope of hydrogen.

questions.question: Why is heavy water heavier than normal water?
questions.explanation: Replacing H-1 with heavier H-2 increases its mass.

questions.question: What is the neutron count in deuterium?
questions.explanation: Deuterium has one neutron, giving it mass number 2.

questions.question: Deuterium naturally occurs in hydrogen at about _____.
questions.explanation: Deuterium exists in extremely small proportions naturally.

questions.question: Almost all naturally occurring carbon is _____.
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 makes up the majority of carbon in nature.

questions.question: Which carbon isotope is used in radiocarbon dating?
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 decays over time and is used to date ancient objects.

questions.question: How many protons are there in all carbon isotopes?
questions.explanation: All carbon isotopes have 6 protons.

questions.question: How many natural isotopes does chlorine have?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes: chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

questions.question: How many protons are present in chlorine-35?
questions.explanation: All chlorine isotopes have 17 protons.

questions.question: Chlorine is fairly soluble in _____.
questions.explanation: Chlorine dissolves moderately in water.

questions.question: Chlorine-37 occurs in nature approximately _____.
questions.explanation: Chlorine-37 is less abundant, about 25%.

questions.question: Which isotope of chlorine is more abundant in nature?
questions.explanation: Chlorine-35 occurs about 75% naturally, making it more abundant.

questions.question: How many neutrons does chlorine-37 have?
questions.explanation: Chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons.

questions.question: Which uranium isotope is used in nuclear reactors and bombs?
questions.explanation: Uranium-235 is fissile and can sustain a nuclear chain reaction.

questions.question: Natural abundance of uranium-234 is approximately _____.
questions.explanation: Uranium-234 is very rare in nature.

questions.question: When uranium-238 decays, it emits _____.
questions.explanation: Uranium-238 emits an alpha particle (helium nucleus) during decay.

questions.question: Energy released by fission of 1 kg uranium-235 is equivalent to burning ____ of coal.
questions.explanation: 1 kg uranium-235 produces energy equal to burning 17,000 kg coal.

questions.question: Relative atomic mass of an element is calculated using its isotopes and their _____.
questions.explanation: The calculation depends on how much each isotope is present in nature.

questions.question: Which carbon isotope has an abundance of 1.1%?
questions.explanation: Carbon-13 accounts for about 1.1% of natural carbon.

questions.question: Iodine-131 is mainly used to diagnose problems in the _____.
questions.explanation: I-131 traces thyroid activity to detect disorders. 99. Iodine-123 is commonly Brain Lungs Bones Liver ○ ○ ○ ○ used for imaging the _____. Answer: (A) Brain

questions.question: Iodine-123 is commonly used for imaging the _____.
questions.explanation: I-123 produces clear images for brain scanning.

questions.question: Which isotope is widely used in radiotherapy to treat cancer?
questions.explanation: Cobalt-60 emits strong gamma rays for tumor treatment.

questions.question: Carbon-14 helps trace the path of carbon during _____.
questions.explanation: C-14 follows carbon movement in photosynthetic reactions.

questions.question: Living organisms constantly absorb carbon-14 because it _____.
questions.explanation: Carbon cycles through air, oceans, and living bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following stops immediately at the moment of death?
questions.explanation: Dead organisms no longer take in radioactive carbon.

questions.question: Cations are usually formed by which type of elements?
questions.explanation: Metals tend to lose electrons easily, leading to cation formation.

questions.question: A cation forms when an atom____.
questions.explanation: Losing electrons results in more protons than electrons, creating a positive ion.

questions.question: What happens to a neutral atom’s electron count when forming a cation?
questions.explanation: A cation forms only when electrons are removed from the atom.

questions.question: A neutral atom becomes a +3 ion after losing electrons. How many electrons were lost?
questions.explanation: The positive charge equals the number of lost electrons.

questions.question: What drives a metal atom to lose electrons and form a cation?
questions.explanation: Metals lose electrons to reach a stable electron configuration like noble gases.

questions.question: When a metal atom forms a cation, its nucleus
questions.explanation: Proton and neutron numbers remain constant during ion formation.

questions.question: An anion forms when an atom______.
questions.explanation: Gaining electrons increases negative charge, forming an anion.

questions.question: Why does gaining electrons make an atom negatively charged?
questions.explanation: More electrons than protons result in a net negative charge.

questions.question: When chlorine gains one electron, it becomes______.
questions.explanation: Gaining one electron gives chlorine a -1 charge.

questions.question: In a neutral atom, protons = electrons. What changes when forming an anion?
questions.explanation: Anions form only when extra electrons are added.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical anion?
questions.explanation: Oxygen commonly gains 2 electrons to form O2-.

questions.question: Why do atoms with high electron affinity easily form anions?
questions.explanation: High electron affinity means the atom readily pulls in electrons to become stable.

questions.question: What happens to the energy of a shell as n increases?
questions.explanation: Electrons in higher shells possess more energy than those in lower shells.

questions.question: Which shell would have the highest energy among the following?
questions.explanation: As n increases, energy rises, so the M shell has more energy than K or L.

questions.question: As the value of n increases, what happens to the electron’s distance from the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Higher shells lie farther from the nucleus, so electron distance increases with n.

questions.question: Which sub-shell exists in the k shell (n=1)?
questions.explanation: The K shell has only 1 sub-shell, labelled as 1s.

questions.question: Which sub-shell can accommodate a maximum of 10 electrons?
questions.explanation: The d sub-shell can hold up to 10 electrons at full capacity.

questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct increasing energy order?
questions.explanation: Energy increases in the sequence 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s and so on, as shown in the Aufbau order.

questions.question: The increasing number of sub-shells in higher shells is due to _____.
questions.explanation: As n increases, the number of allowed sub-shells also increases (n sub-shells per shell).

questions.question: Why does the 4s sub- shell fill before the 3d sub- shell?

options.A: 4s is physica closer to th nucleus

questions.explanation: Even though it is in a higher shell, 4s has slightly lower energy than 3d, so it fills first.

questions.question: Why does the M shell contain a 3d sub-shell but the L shell does not contain a 2d sub-shell?

options.B: to      d sub-shell start from n
options.C: d sub-shel s cannot hol = 3 electrons

questions.explanation: Quantum rules allow d sub-shells to exist only from the third energy level (n = 3).

questions.question: In an ion symbol, a 2+ charge indicates the atom has _____.
questions.explanation: A positive charge means electrons were lost since losing negative particles makes the ion positive.

questions.question: The atomic number is always equal to the number of _____.
questions.explanation: Atomic number uniquely identifies an element by counting its protons.
